title: Dunder protocol contracts
prompt_md: Dunder methods are contracts the interpreter relies on. Getting one half-right — `__eq__` without `__hash__`, `__enter__` without `__exit__` — produces objects that look fine and misbehave in a container or a `with` block. Reason about the contracts, not just the syntax.

questions.stem_md: You add `__eq__` to a class so two points with the same coordinates compare equal. You define nothing else. What happens when you put an instance in a `set`?

options.md: `TypeError: unhashable type` — defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to `None`.
It works, using identity-based hashing as before.
It works, and equal points collapse to one entry automatically.
`RecursionError`, because `__eq__` calls `__hash__`.

questions.explanation_md: Defining `__eq__` makes the class unhashable unless you also define `__hash__` — Python sets `__hash__ = None` to enforce the invariant that equal objects must hash equally. Redefining equality without redefining hashing would break that, so the language removes hashing rather than let you ship the bug. Set `__hash__` explicitly (often over the same fields), or use `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, or `eq=True` with a hashable design.

sources.locator: object.__hash__ — set to None when __eq__ is defined

questions.stem_md: You will implement only **one** of `__repr__` and `__str__`. Which, and why?

options.md: `__repr__` — `__str__` falls back to it, so one method covers both `print()` and the debugger/`repr()`.
`__str__` — `__repr__` falls back to it.
Either; they are aliases.
`__str__`, because `__repr__` is only for subclasses.

questions.explanation_md: `__str__` defaults to `__repr__`, not the other way round, so implementing `__repr__` alone gives you a sensible result everywhere — logs, tracebacks, the REPL, and `print()`. Aim for an unambiguous `__repr__` (ideally one that looks like the constructor call); add `__str__` only when end-user display should differ from the developer view.

questions.stem_md: Which statements about the context-manager protocol (`with obj:`) are true?

options.md: `__exit__` runs even if the `with` body raises.
`__exit__` returning a truthy value suppresses the exception.
The value bound by `as` is whatever `__enter__` returns.
If `__enter__` is defined but `__exit__` is not, `with` still works.
`__exit__` receives the exception type, value and traceback (or three `None`s).

questions.explanation_md: `__enter__` and `__exit__` are a pair: cleanup runs on both the normal and the exceptional path, `as` binds `__enter__`'s return value, and `__exit__` sees the exception triple and can swallow it by returning truthy (usually a mistake — do it deliberately). Defining only `__enter__` raises `AttributeError` on the `with`; both are required. `contextlib.contextmanager` lets you write the pair as one generator with a `try/finally`.

questions.stem_md: A class defines `__getitem__(self, i)` that returns `self.data[i]` and raises `IndexError` past the end, but no `__iter__`. Can you write `for x in obj`?

options.md: Yes — the old sequence protocol lets `for` call `__getitem__` with 0, 1, 2… until `IndexError`.
No — iteration strictly requires `__iter__`.
Yes, but only if `__len__` is also defined.
No — `__getitem__` is only for `obj[i]`, never for `for`.

questions.explanation_md: If `__iter__` is absent, `for` falls back to the legacy sequence protocol: call `__getitem__(0)`, `__getitem__(1)`, … and stop on `IndexError`. It works, but `__iter__` is clearer and required for non-integer-indexable iterables, so prefer defining it. The point is that `for` is protocol-driven, not type-driven — several dunders can satisfy it.

questions.stem_md: You want value objects that compare and hash by their fields, and are safe as dict keys. Which approaches give you a correct, consistent `__eq__`/`__hash__` pair?

options.md: `@dataclass(frozen=True)`
`@dataclass(eq=True)` with mutable fields, left unfrozen
Hand-write `__eq__` and `__hash__` over the same tuple of fields, and don't mutate those fields after creation
`typing.NamedTuple` with the fields

questions.explanation_md: The invariant is that equal objects hash equally *and* the hash never changes while the object is a key. `frozen=True` and `NamedTuple` are immutable, so both fall out for free; hand-writing both over the same fields works only if you treat those fields as immutable. Option (b) is the trap: `eq=True` without `frozen=True` sets `__hash__ = None`, so the object is unhashable — and if you forced a hash over mutable fields, mutating one would strand the entry in the wrong bucket.

hints.md: Think of each dunder as one side of a contract the interpreter enforces. The recurring theme: some come in pairs (`__eq__`/`__hash__`, `__enter__`/`__exit__`) and defining one without the other leaves a broken object.

Key invariants: equal objects must hash equally, so Python nulls `__hash__` when you define `__eq__` alone; `__str__` falls back to `__repr__` (so implement `__repr__`); `with` needs both enter and exit, and exit runs on the error path too; and `for` will use `__iter__` or fall back to `__getitem__`-until-`IndexError`.

Answers: (1) `TypeError: unhashable` — `__eq__` alone nulls `__hash__`. (2) implement `__repr__`; `__str__` falls back to it. (3) true: exit-on-raise, truthy-suppresses, `as` binds enter's return, exit gets the exception triple — false: enter-only does not work. (4) yes, via the `__getitem__`/`IndexError` fallback. (5) `frozen=True`, hand-written-over-immutable-fields, and `NamedTuple`; not `eq=True` unfrozen.
